notes.title: Who lives here?
notes.body: A forest is a network of habitats. Its canopy, bark, roots and leaf litter provide different places for living things. Keeping trees standing is important, but protecting biodiversity also means caring for the connected forest around them. These illustrated trees do not identify species recorded in this research cell.
notes.takeaway: A forest is more than a tree count.

notes.title: Where is the carbon?
notes.body: Trees take in carbon as they grow, but a forest's carbon is not only in its trunks. It is also found in roots, soil and dead wood. Forest management and climate action are connected. This illustration explains that connection; it does not estimate carbon stored or emissions avoided at the selected location.
notes.takeaway: Some of a forest's carbon is out of sight.
notes.sourceTitle: FAO · Forests and climate change; United Nations · Goal 13

notes.title: Why monitor a forest?
notes.body: Monitoring resources are limited. MLBorneo studies which areas should receive attention first. The forest area assessed in 2018, the research priority ranking, and changes recorded in 2019–2020 describe different things. A high ranking does not mean loss is certain. Monitoring also does not prove that forest has been protected or that loss has been avoided.
notes.takeaway: Monitoring helps direct attention. It is not a protection guarantee.
notes.sourceTitle: MLBorneo frozen research records; United Nations · Goal 15
